readerTitle: Same deal, two owners: why one should say no
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소형 완구 도매상 vs 지역 유통사, 레스토랑 2호점) + 실제 연구 (Kelly, 1956 베팅 크기 공식)를 짧게 언급 · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 같은 거래라도 손실이 사업을 끝낼 수 있는지에 따라 좋은 베팅이 되기도 하고 위험한 베팅이 되기도 한다. 평균보다 먼저 '실패해도 살아남는가'를 묻는다.
misconception: 기대값이 플러스이고 이길 확률이 높으면 크게 걸수록 좋다.

sources.text: Kelly, J. L. (1956). A New Interpretation of Information Rate. Bell System Technical Journal, 35(4), 917–926.
모든 사업 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 차트 수치: 소형 도매상 $40,000 − $30,000 = $10,000, 지역 유통사 $400,000 − $30,000 = $370,000. 실패 시 재고 가치를 0으로 단순화했습니다(카드에는 'nearly worthless').
반복 확률: 다섯 번 모두 성공할 확률 0.8^5 = 0.32768, 한 번 이상 실패할 확률 1 − 0.328 ≈ 0.67(67%). 각 거래가 독립이라는 가정입니다.
Kelly(1956)가 Bell Labs에서 장기 성장률을 최대화하는 베팅 비율을 제시했다는 서술을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 '자금 대비 베팅 크기를 정하는 아이디어'로만 일반적으로 적었습니다.

cards.title: Same deal, two owners: why one should say no
body: Two businesses are offered the exact same deal. It wins four times out of five, and on average it makes money.
For one owner, it's a smart bet. For the other, it's the most dangerous decision of the year. The deal is the same. The difference is what a loss would do to each of them.

image.label: Two shop owners holding the same contract, one standing on a wide platform, one on a narrow ledge
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 두 사업가가 똑같은 계약서를 들고 있음. 한 명은 넓고 튼튼한 받침대 위에, 다른 한 명은 좁은 절벽 끝에 서 있음. 계약서는 동일하게 보이도록. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A big holiday lot at a bargain price.
body: You run a small toy wholesaler with $40,000 in the bank. A supplier offers a large lot of holiday stock for $30,000.
You think there's an 80% chance you resell it for $50,000. If the trend fades, there's a 20% chance it's nearly worthless. What do you do?

options.text: Buy the whole lot. The odds are clearly in your favor
options.feedback: The average outcome is good, but one bad season leaves you with $10,000 and bills to pay. You'd be betting the business on a four-in-five chance.

options.text: Buy about a third of the lot, for roughly $10,000
options.feedback: You give up some upside, but a flop now costs $10,000 instead of $30,000. You stay in business to make the next bet.

options.text: Pass. Anything that can lose money is too risky
options.feedback: You're safe, but you skip a bet that pays off most of the time. The question isn't whether you can lose. It's how much.

cards.title: On average, the deal looks good.
body: Taken many times, this deal earns about $10,000 each time. That's what expected value says. But you don't get many tries if the first flop empties your bank account.

cards.title: Now give the same deal to a bigger business.
body: A regional distributor with $400,000 in the bank gets the identical offer. Here's the cash each business has before the deal, and after a flop.
cards.callout: Same odds, same dollars. For one, a dent. For the other, possibly the end.

cards.title: The risk of ruin
body: **Risk of ruin** is the chance that a loss leaves you unable to keep going: no cash for wages, no money for stock, no business.
Ordinary losses hurt and then heal. Ruin is different, because it also ends every future bet. So a good average isn't enough. First ask: *if this goes wrong, am I still standing?*

image.label: A board game path where one square sends the player off the board entirely
image.brief: 보드게임 판 일러스트. 대부분의 칸은 '+' 또는 '−' 작은 숫자, 한 칸만 판 밖으로 떨어지는 구멍이 있고 'Game over' 라벨. 플레이어 말이 그 칸 근처에 서 있음.

cards.softwareNote: A startup with 12 months of runway that spends 9 months of cash on one launch campaign faces the same math. If the launch flops, there's no money left to learn from it and try again.

cards.title: Rare bad luck becomes likely with repetition.
body: A 20% chance of a flop sounds small. But businesses face bets like this again and again.
Take this kind of deal five times, and the chance of at least one flop is about **67%**. If a single flop is fatal, you probably won't make it through five.
That's why professional bettors and investors size each bet to their total funds, an idea John Kelly worked out at Bell Labs in 1956.

cards.title: Ruin often sits outside the deal itself.
body: The question is the same everywhere: what is the worst realistic case, and can you survive it? Watch for these:
list: **One customer** who makes up most of your sales
**A personal guarantee** on a lease or loan
**A single supplier** you can't replace quickly
**One big bet** that uses most of your cash
cards.callout: The fix is usually sizing, not skipping: make it smaller, shorter or shared.

cards.title: You can be too careful, and too sure of the worst case.
body: Refusing every bet that can hurt has a cost too. A business that never risks anything rarely grows. The goal is to keep losses survivable, not to avoid all losses.
Also, worst cases are often worse than owners guess. A flop can arrive together with a slow season or a late customer payment. Leave room beyond the worst case you can picture.

cards.title: Now it's a second restaurant.
body: Your restaurant is doing well and you have $60,000 saved. A landlord offers a great corner spot. The fit-out costs $50,000, and the 10-year lease needs your personal guarantee.
You expect it to succeed more often than not. What do you do?

options.text: Sign. A busy corner and a proven menu make it a good bet
options.feedback: It may well work. But if it fails, the fit-out money is gone and you personally owe years of rent, which could sink the first restaurant too.

options.text: Push for a shorter lease without a personal guarantee, or test the area with a pop-up first
options.feedback: You may pay more rent or grow more slowly, but a failure becomes a setback instead of the end. The first restaurant stays safe.

options.text: Skip it and keep all the cash in the bank
options.feedback: Nothing can go wrong, but you also pass on a likely win. The problem was the size of the downside, not the idea.

cards.title: Never take a bet you can't afford to lose.
body: A good average only helps if you survive long enough to collect it. Size each bet so the worst case still leaves you able to play again.
**Try it today:** list your three biggest commitments. For each, write the worst realistic outcome and how many months of cash you'd have left.
